chapter: Clubs, publishers, unions and life in Denver
title: Dealing with music publishers: selling outright and exclusive contracts
summary: Horace sold some originals outright, signed an exclusive contract that let tunes gather dust, and learned to demand cancellation clauses; Fletcher was too trusting.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: Uh-huh. Okay. This is sort of switching. You've had some music published, I mean some of your own compositions. Is that correct?
What sort of dealings did you have with music publishers? How was that done?

Well, there were a few companies that I dealt with that I sold the originals outright, unfortunately, before I got hip, you know, to what I should have done. There were others that we had a deal where there it was a commission thing going on, you know. And then -- let's see -- there was a company here back that wanted you to sign exclusively with them, and you couldn't write for anybody else, any original tunes, one of those things. I signed a contract with a company like that. I think it was Mills Music long ago, (unintelligible), but I found out that that was a handicap to me because a lot of times you write tunes, and if you didn't record them, they'd put them on the shelf, and they gather

dust, you know, one of those things, and then you'd go down and you'd try to jack them up on it, and there's nothing you could do. You're contracted. So you're just stuck; the only thing is sweat out until it was one of those things. And you would do it until your contract was terminated, you know, and then if they wanted you to sign, you know better. You're crazy (unintelligible) if you did it, you know?

So the next contract, if you'd have any, you'd have certain stipulations in there that, if they didn't do certain things, why the contract would be null and void or you'd have the option to cancel it and go with somebody else. But you had to learn all these kind of things, you know, because you were dealing with some real pros, you know, that knew all the answers. And this is one of the things, unfortunately, that Fletcher wasn't well versed in, you know, because he's the type of easy going guy would take guys at their word, you know, and then they'd, you know, so called -- stick a knife in his back too, you know, so he wasn't able to give me that information in time for me not to be a victim too. But you learn quick.
